title: Predictable default passwords for imported users
description: Bulk-imported student accounts are created with the shared password `password`, while bulk-imported teacher accounts are created with the shared password `password123`. Both flows also set `password_changed_at` to the import time. The login flow accepts non-email identifiers as the `nis` credential and email-format identifiers as `email`. An unauthenticated attacker who knows or guesses a student's NIS, or an imported teacher's email address such as the generated `<nip>@sekolah.sch.id`, can log in with the default password if the imported user has not manually changed it.
root_cause: StudentsImport in app/Imports/StudentsImport.php and TeachersImport in app/Imports/TeachersImport.php do not generate unique one-time credentials or force first-login rotation, allowing account takeover of imported users with shared default passwords.
intended_behavior: Bulk import should onboard student and teacher accounts without leaving any account usable with a shared known password; each imported user should receive a unique secret or be forced to set a password before gaining normal access.

trace.description: The admin route group exposes POST /admin/students/import to authenticated admin users when the import_data feature is enabled.
The student import controller validates the uploaded spreadsheet and imports it with StudentsImport.
StudentsImport creates a hash for the literal shared password `password` before processing rows.
StudentsImport creates the user using the spreadsheet NIS and stores the shared default password hash, while setting password_changed_at to now.
The admin route group exposes POST /admin/teachers/import to authenticated admin users when the import_data feature is enabled.

TeachersImport creates new teacher users using the spreadsheet NIP, either the spreadsheet email or a generated <nip>@sekolah.sch.id email, and the literal shared password `password123`, while setting password_changed_at to now.

The login controller attempts authentication with the submitted identifier and password; non-email identifiers are mapped to the nis field and email-format identifiers are mapped to the email field, so imported student NIS values and imported teacher email values can be used with the shared default passwords.

conditions.description: The target account must have been created through the student or teacher import flow and not manually changed its password afterward.
Login by NIS/NIP must be enabled; this is the default according to the login controller setting lookup.

execution.attacker_perspective: Unauthenticated internet or intranet user who knows or can guess a student's NIS or a teacher's NIP.
instructions: Obtain or guess a student NIS, or obtain/derive an imported teacher email address such as <nip>@sekolah.sch.id from the target institution.
Submit the login form using the identifier as the `email` field and the relevant shared default password.
If the account was imported and unchanged, follow the role redirect into the authenticated dashboard.
execution.expected_result: The attacker receives an authenticated session as the imported student or teacher account.

remediation.strategy: Replace shared default passwords with unique one-time credentials and enforce first-login password rotation for imported users.

code_changes.fixed_code: Generate a per-user temporary password with Str::password(16), store only Hash::make($temporaryPassword), and set password_changed_at to null or a must_change_password flag.
Generate a per-user temporary password with Str::password(16), store only Hash::make($temporaryPassword), and set password_changed_at to null or a must_change_password flag.
After Auth::attempt, check the force-change marker and redirect to a password setup route before granting normal role dashboard access.

likelihood.reason: The attack requires an imported account and knowledge of an identifier, but NIS/NIP values are commonly known or guessable in school environments.

impact.reason: Successful exploitation gives full access to the targeted student or teacher account, but does not directly bypass into admin or platform-wide privileges.

confidence.reason: The import code, stored password values, login credential mapping, and lack of force-change enforcement were traced directly in source files.

title: Password reset reveals whether an email exists
description: The public password reset endpoint returns a success response when Password::broker()->sendResetLink reports RESET_LINK_SENT and an error response otherwise. An unauthenticated attacker can submit candidate email addresses to distinguish registered accounts from unknown addresses.
root_cause: sendResetLinkEmail in app/Http/Controllers/Auth/ForgotPasswordController.php does not return a uniform response for valid and invalid reset targets, allowing email account enumeration.
intended_behavior: Password reset should not reveal whether a submitted email belongs to an account; user-facing responses should be identical for valid and invalid addresses.

trace.description: The public POST /forgot-password route calls ForgotPasswordController::sendResetLinkEmail without authentication.
The controller returns a success flash for RESET_LINK_SENT and an error response for other broker statuses.

execution.attacker_perspective: Unauthenticated user probing whether target email addresses are registered.
instructions: Submit the password reset form with a candidate email address.
Compare the response category: success indicates a registered address, while an error indicates an unregistered address.
execution.expected_result: The attacker can build a list of valid account email addresses.

remediation.strategy: Always return the same user-facing message from the password reset request endpoint, regardless of broker status.

code_changes.fixed_code: Call Password::broker()->sendResetLink($request->only('email')); then always return back()->with('success', __('If the address exists, a password reset link has been sent.'));

likelihood.reason: The endpoint is public and the response difference is direct.

impact.reason: The issue reveals account existence only; it does not grant access without another attack.

confidence.reason: The public route and divergent response branch were verified directly in source.
